answer_text:
Here is a comprehensive overview of the **causes of coagulopathy**:

---

## 🩸 What is Coagulopathy?

Coagulopathy is a medical condition characterized by an inability of blood to coagulate or clot (hypocoagulation). It is also known as a bleeding disorder because an inability of blood to clot can result in excessive or prolonged bleeding of wounds.

Coagulopathies refer to a range of conditions that affect the blood's ability to clot normally. In a healthy person, platelets and clotting factors work together to stop bleeding when a blood vessel is damaged. In coagulopathies, one or more of these factors are missing, defective, or overactive. As a result, the blood may not clot when needed, or it may clot excessively, leading to complications such as deep vein thrombosis or stroke.

---

## 📌 Major Causes of Coagulopathy

### 1. 🧬 Genetic / Inherited Causes
Genetic differences, deficiencies, or mutations can cause different types of coagulation disorders. Biological parents can pass down these mutations, and in some cases, they can also occur after birth.

Some people are born with defective or missing clotting factors. Conditions like Hemophilia A and B, and Von Willebrand disease, are among the most common inherited coagulopathies. These conditions can cause prolonged bleeding even from minor injuries.

Thrombocytopenia, von Willebrand disease (vWD), and hemophilia are the leading causes of coagulopathy. The worldwide incidence of vWD, hemophilia A, and hemophilia B affects approximately 125, 20.6, and 5.3 cases per million populations, respectively.

---

### 2. 🫀 Liver Disease
Hemostasis is intimately related to liver function, because most coagulation factors are synthesized by liver parenchymal cells. The extent of coagulation abnormalities depends upon the degree of disturbed liver function.

Acute or chronic hepatocellular diseases may display decreases in the vitamin K-dependent factors (prothrombin; factors VII, IX, and X; proteins C and S). Patients with hepatic failure may present with the entire spectrum of factor deficiencies and may even develop disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC).

---

### 3. 🥬 Vitamin K Deficiency
Vitamin K deficiency affects a variety of vitamin K-dependent factors, including factors II, VII, IX, and X, as well as proteins C & S. Vitamin K is primarily synthesized by colonic bacteria and can be obtained from dietary sources such as green leafy vegetables.

Vitamin K deficiency can be due to deficient biosynthesis in the intestinal tract in various pathological situations such as: medicine-induced intestinal dysbacteriosis (especially after antibiotic treatment), enteropathies accompanied by heavy diarrhea, mechanical jaundice, prematurity of newborns, and severe liver disease.

Vitamin K deficiency typically accounts for ≥30% of all coagulopathy referrals, and is particularly common among infants but can occur at any age.

---

### 4. 🔬 Disseminated Intravascular Coagulation (DIC)
Abnormalities in DIC may be due to deficient synthesis of coagulation factors in hepatocellular failure, failure of vitamin K absorption, and DIC itself. DIC occurs in hepatocellular failure because the liver cells are normally responsible for clearing activated products of the coagulation and fibrinolytic enzyme systems.

---

### 5. 💊 Anticoagulant Medications
Taking blood thinners, like heparin or warfarin, may increase the risk of coagulopathy. These medicines prevent dangerous clots but may lead to excess bleeding if a person is injured.

---

### 6. 🩺 Acquired Platelet Dysfunction
Non-inherited causes of coagulopathy include acquired platelet dysfunction (e.g., from nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug use and renal disease), idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura, or acquired factor consumption.

---

### 7. 🏥 Trauma and Surgery
Coagulopathy may be caused by conditions such as uncontrolled bleeding from anticoagulation therapy, trauma, surgery, delivery, and disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC).

---

### 8. 🦠 Infectious and Chronic Diseases
Infectious diseases such as malaria, diarrhea, intestinal helminthiasis, acute respiratory infections, tuberculosis, and chronic diseases can cause coagulopathy. They can cause blood coagulation factor deficiency, production of blood coagulation factor inhibitors, and thrombocytopenia.

---

## 🗂️ Summary Table

| Category | Examples |
|---|---|
| **Genetic/Inherited** | Hemophilia A & B, Von Willebrand Disease |
| **Liver Disease** | Cirrhosis, Hepatic failure |
| **Vitamin K Deficiency** | Malnutrition, Antibiotic use, Cholestasis |
| **DIC** | Sepsis, Obstetric emergencies, Malignancy |
| **Medications** | Warfarin, Heparin, NSAIDs |
| **Platelet Disorders** | Thrombocytopenia, ITP, Renal disease |
| **Trauma/Surgery** | Major trauma, Massive hemorrhage |
| **Infections/Chronic Disease** | Malaria, Tuberculosis |

---

> ⚠️ **Clinical Note:** Coagulopathy may cause uncontrolled internal or external bleeding. Left untreated, uncontrolled bleeding may cause damage to joints, muscles, or internal organs and may be life-threatening. Early diagnosis and treatment are essential.
